title: Does the next half take as long?
hook: Half gone in 10 minutes. Is the next half gone in 10 more?

knows: that a half-life is the time for half of something to go (half-life lesson)
doesNotKnow: that for some reactions the half-life is not fixed: it lengthens as the reactant thins

misconception: Every reaction has one fixed half-life.
objective: The learner can explain that a second-order reaction that halves from 80 to 40 mmol/L in 10 min takes 20 min to halve again (then 40 min), because two molecules must meet and meetings get rarer as the reactant thins, while a first-order reaction keeps one half-life.

claims.text: A second-order reaction that takes 10 min to go from 80 to 40 mmol/L takes about 20 min to go from 40 to 20 mmol/L, and about 40 min more to reach 10 mmol/L.
claims.source: Integrated rate law 1/[A] = 1/[A]0 + kt: k = (1/40 - 1/80)/10 = 1/800 L/(mmol min); t(20) - t(40) = (1/20 - 1/40) x 800 = 20 min; t(10) - t(20) = 40 min (node; Demo.tsx timeTo()). | Builder revision v5 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): (r7) The reveal now quotes a persistent '2nd-order waits' row, waitRow(2) = wait(2,1..seen[2]) joined ', ' + ' min' (gate: seen[2] >= 2, so '10, 20 min' or '10, 20, 40 min'), instead of the wait bars, which only show the current order. Builder statement, not self-verified. | FC pass 26 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. k = (1/40 - 1/80)/10 = 1/800; t(40) = 10, t(20) = 30, t(10) = 70 min, waits 10, 20, 40. Own Euler integration of dA/dt = -kA^2 from 80: reaches 40, 20, 10 at 10.00, 30.00, 70.00 min. waitRow(2) re-run in node: "10, 20 min" (seen 2) and "10, 20, 40 min" (seen 3); the reveal needs second-twice, so seen[2] >= 2 and the quoted row is never shorter than "10, 20 min". Rows persist across order switches (no reset control).

claims.text: A second-order reaction's half-life grows as the concentration falls; each half takes twice as long as the last.
claims.source: t1/2 = 1/(k[A]0) for rate = k[A]^2 (Atkins & de Paula, Physical Chemistry, ch. on chemical kinetics, table of integrated rate laws). | REVISION v2 2026-10-14: text edited to match stage; needs re-check. | Builder revision v7 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, learner r8 / W-291): reveal cut to fit the phone: 'Your 2nd-order waits read 10, 20 min: each half takes twice as long as the last. With half as much left to lose at a quarter of the rate, each wait doubles. In 1st order the rate only halved (1/2 -> 1/4), so the half-life stays fixed.' The 'As the line under it said' sentence is gone. claims.text: In a second-order reaction of this kind, two reactant molecules must meet, so the rate goes with the concentration squared; halving the concentration makes meetings four times rarer (rate 1/4 of the start after one halving, 1/16 after two). In first order the rate halves each time.
claims.source: Rate = k[A]^2 for an elementary bimolecular step 2A -> products (Atkins & de Paula, ch. on kinetics). Order is measured, not always from the equation; the lesson's reaction is stated to be second order. | REVISION v2 2026-10-14: text edited to match stage; needs re-check. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v3, wave D r5 revision by demo-builder): learner-visible sentence changed; needs a fresh check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Pass 22: rate = k[A]^2: (1/2)^2 = 1/4, (1/4)^2 = 1/16; first order 1/2, 1/4. claims.text: Each halving leaves half as much to lose; in 2nd order it goes at a quarter of the rate, so the wait doubles; in 1st order at half the rate, so the wait stays the same. (Stage line: 'Each halving: ½ as much left to lose, at ¼ the rate → 2× the wait' / '... at ½ the rate → same wait'.)
claims.source: Scaling: for rate = k[A]^m, the time to go from c to c/2 scales as c^(1−m) (integrated rate law). m = 2: halving c doubles the wait; m = 1: the wait is unchanged. The rate at the start of each halving is (1/2)^m of the one before, which is the 1/4 or 1/2 on the line. The amount lost per halving is c/2, half the previous. Stage text in Demo.tsx (.why line). | Added 2026-10-14 (v3) by demo-builder. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Pass 22: derivation. Each halving of a power-law decay is the previous one rescaled: concentration x1/2 at every matching point, so rate x(1/2)^m throughout; time = amount/rate scales by (1/2)/(1/2)^m = 2^(m-1): x2 for m = 2, x1 for m = 1. Exact, not an approximation. Matches the .why line text in Demo.tsx and own integration (c4). | Builder revision v7 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, learner r8 / W-291): reveal cut to fit the phone: 'Your 2nd-order waits read 10, 20 min: each half takes twice as long as the last. recall.question: A second-order reaction takes 5 min to fall from 100 to 50 mmol/L. About how long does the next fall, from 50 to 25 mmol/L, take?
recall.why: For a second-order reaction the half-life is 1/(k[A]); halving [A] doubles it.
